title: The Name on the Slate
passages:
The sky over the Kettle went the color of a wet coin an hour before noon, and the season bell up on the arcology's high tower started its slow count, one strike every ten seconds, the way it did when a channel was about to close and everybody's unfinished business became everybody's emergency. Wren had the chart-space hatch propped open to let the heat out, which also let the rain in sideways, and she worked with one shoulder hunched against it.

The slate sat on her bench in a puddle of its own rust. A slate is the recorder a diver clips to the chest strap of his harness: it logs his voice and his depth, hour on hour, so that a topside tech can rebuild a dive that nobody came up to describe. This one had gone into Mercy General's flooded stairwell fourteen months ago with Ivo Salas strapped inside the same harness, and it had come out of the pocket at forty-two meters crusted the green-gray of a hull plate.

"Give it here." Bayo leaned in the hatchway, dry, which was more than the rest of them could manage. "I've a hand for old gear."

"You've a hand for old gear the way you've got a berth," Dey said, from the deck where he was sitting with his back against the bench leg, breathing on his own lungs, no scrubber on his chest, because Teo had that. "Warm. And brief."

"I'll take warm."

Wren didn't look up. She had the case cracked and a wire brush going along the contact strip, the little copper comb that carries the charge out of the cell and into the log. Salt gets into everything. Salt gets into a cell and eats it from the inside until what's left is a brick with delusions.

"Talk to me," Salas said. He was standing at her shoulder with his arms folded, a big man gone careful in his movements, watching a piece of his own year get scraped clean. "Is it holding anything?"

"It's fourteen months in seawater. It's holding rust." She flicked rust onto the deck. "Cell's supposed to be flat. Dead as a doornail. That's the whole design — no charge, no log, no ghosts, so nobody spends a week listening to a drowned man's last shift."

"That's considerate of it," Bayo said.

"That's *law*, is what that is." She thumbed the cell free, wiped the contacts down with a rag that had stopped being a rag years ago, and seated it again. "Don't lean on my bench."

In the corner Nia had folded herself down beside the crate where Teo slept with his mouth open, and she was turning his berth-card over and over in her fist — berth four-oh-eight, the arcology's own stock, stamped and paid — like a woman checking a coin she already knew was good. Outside, the bell counted. Inside, the reader waited: a steel box bolted to the bench with a slot in the front and a spool behind glass, a cradle, the thing that plays back what went down with a diver so the top of the world can hear it.

Wren closed the slate into the slot, wiped her hands, and reached for the switch.

The charge gauge on the cradle face was a strip of nine little windows, and it was dark, and it stayed dark for as long as it took her to breathe twice. Then the first window went amber.

Then the second.

"It's reading a charge," she said.

"Good," said Bayo.

"No." Wren sat back. In fourteen months of salt water that cell should have been a stone, and a stone does not have three windows and climbing. Behind the glass, unasked, with nobody's thumb on anything, the spool began to turn.
